title: Chapter 118 – The Registry Strikes
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Qin Hao]

Three winters later. The shortest night of the thirty-fifth year.

Qin Hao has kept the Gate for sixty-three years, and he knows to the stone how much of it is left in him.

He sits on his stool at the mouth of the stair in the gray light before the Offering, with his hands knotted on his knees and his white beard combed over his chest, and counts the stones of the Gate Court the way another man might count beads. Nine hundred and twelve paving stones. Twenty-two lamp-posts. One wall, forty feet long and as thick as a house, of gray granite blocks the size of oxen, closing the stair from the sky. He has swept that wall every morning of his life. He knows the grain of every block. He knows the single hairline crack, the width of a straw, on the ninth course from the top, where the damp gets in. He has never, in six decades, had the courage to ask what the wall is for.

He is eighty-eight. He weighs less than a boy. His hands shake, in the cold, like leaves.

Sixty years of credit, he thinks. I spent it in a single morning, at a table, for a young man I had met twice. It was the best use I ever made of it.

The Gate Court is already filling. They have been coming since the third watch: the Halls in their colors, the clans in their lines, the Elders in their cushions, the Court in black. By dawn there will be a thousand. By dusk there will be two. They stand in a wide half circle, five ranks deep, with the snow on their shoulders, and nobody speaks. A man does not speak at the Grand Offering. It is the one night of the tenth year when the Sect keeps silence, and each member, from the Head's chair to the least kitchen boy, comes to the foot of the mountain to give back to the Gate what it has been lent.

That is what he was taught. He has never once believed it.

* * *

He has not been idle, and he has not been lonely, which is a thing he did not expect to learn at eighty-eight.

For three years the old man has been a spider in a corner of a very large web. He has drawn up the order of the Halls and the order of the clans. He has written the roll of the Court. He has visited every Elder in turn, in his black cloak, with his stool carried by a runner, and asked each one the same question, and watched what the face did before the answer.

Do you wish the Gate opened?

Eleven said no at once. Nine said no after a moment. Four said they had no opinion and one of those, he thinks, was lying. Three said yes. And one, the Elder of the Hall of Weights, said nothing at all, and wept.

He knows the roll of the Court by heart now. He knows which are Numbers.

There are forty-one of them, in the Sect, by his count. Nineteen are in the Court itself, in clerks' desks and wardens' posts, in the Treasury and the Hall of Weights and the Hall of Law. Twelve are in the Inner Court. Ten are in the lower town, in trades and stalls. Mu's name was the forty-first. The old Law Elder had come to him in the autumn, gray and shaking, and laid his own number on the table like a debt. Strike it from the roll, he said. And put me on the line.

Qin Hao had said: You will die.

Yes, said Mu. But I will know what for.

He had wept, then, which Qin Hao had not expected. Qin Hao had not expected to be moved either. He had sat for a long time looking at the other man's bent head and thinking that the Rule was a cage after all, but that sometimes, if the bars were strong enough, a thing inside could stand up.

* * *

The Halls arrive in order, as the old precedent says.

First the Pill Hall, in the gray-green of herbs, with Bai at its head in a robe he has not worn in thirty years, waddling and furious and chewing the stem of a plum. Then the Sutra Hall, in white, with Ye in her stiff old Elder's cloak, leaning on her stick, her face as blank as paper. Then the Law Hall, in black, led by Mu, who walks as though every step were measured. The Treasury follows, without its Elder. The Hall of Weights follows, with its head bowed.

And then the Cloud Peak Hall, a column in sky blue, with Shen Yuxian at its head, and beside her, with a stick, a thin white-bearded old man who has not been seen in public for seven years. A murmur runs through the crowd like wind in a field. Yuxian does not look at it. She takes her place beside the Law Hall and folds her hands.

The clans come next. The Tan, in their ink-colored robes, Ruyan at the head with her jade ring. The Green Pine families. The Red Ridge remnants who swore. The Zhao, fifty-one, in brown, with Yao at their head and a young man of eighteen at his side who looks about at the faces with a curiosity that is almost unseemly.

And last of all, when the sun has dropped behind the ridge and the lamps are being lit, the Garden Hall.

It comes up the lane in a double file, three hundred and four strong. Wenyuan leads it, tall and stooped, in a clean gray robe with a jade pin in his hair. Qinghe walks at his side. Behind them come Hu, enormous and silent, and Feng with his plain dark blade, and Bei, and Yue with her black braid pinned up like a woman's. Below them march the guards, nineteen, in brown, and the school, and the stall, and the little children on their mothers' hips. They take their place in the front rank, on the left of the stair, in a line that is straighter than any other, and Wenyuan turns, and looks, once, at Qin Hao on his stool.

Qin Hao inclines his head.

Three hundred and four, he thinks. When I first knew them there were nine.

* * *

They bring the Head at dusk.

It is the one thing he has not been able to stop. Eight Numbers in plum-colored robes come down the long stair from the ridge, bearing on their shoulders a litter of white jade, and on the litter, tranquil and heavy and entirely still, lies the man who has ruled the Azure Cloud Sect for thirty-one years. His eyes are closed. His hands are folded. A small gold chain lies on his breast. From his brow, a single cord of gray silk rises into the dusk, and runs up the mountain.

They set the litter down at the head of the Court, before the wall.

Behind them, unhurried, walking alone down the last flights of the long stair with a lantern in its hand, comes the Keeper.

Qin Hao has never seen it. He has heard, as every man in the Sect has heard, that there is a Keeper of the Roll and that it has no face. He had assumed that to be a figure of speech. It is not. The figure that comes down the stair is tall and slender, robed to the ground in dark plum, and over its head and shoulders hangs a veil of black gauze so fine that the lantern light passes through it, and shows nothing. No profile. No hair. Only a shadow where a face should be.

It walks without sound. The hush of two thousand people deepens until he can hear his own heart.

It stops at the foot of the stair. It sets down the lantern. And it raises one gloved hand to the snow, palm up, in the old gesture of a man receiving a gift.

"The Offering," says a soft, even, genderless voice, "is begun."

It is the Nameless. Qin Hao did not see it step forward from the Keeper's shadow. It stands now at the head of the litter, a tall plum figure in a mask of white lacquer, with its hands folded in its sleeves, and it speaks to the whole of the Court without raising its voice.

"For six hundred years, the Gate has been kept. For six hundred years, the Sect has paid the keeping. The House has asked nothing, and the Sect has given nothing, and in the silence between them the work has been done. This night the House closes its account. It asks only that the Sect hear its last offer, and decide."

"What offer?" says Qin Hao.

His voice is dry and cracked. It carries to the back of the crowd. The mask turns toward him.

"Elder Qin," it says. "You have kept the stair. You have the right to speak."

"I have a right to ask what is being offered."

"The Gate," says the Nameless. "The House asks that it be given. Freely, by the vote of the Sect, in the presence of its Head. The Head's voice will be cast by proxy, as it has been for eleven years. The Council's will be cast by roll. And when the vote is counted, the House will open the Gate and take upon itself the burden that the Sect has borne, and the Sect will be released."

"Released from what?"

"From the Gate."

Silence.

"And the Operator?" asks Qin Hao.

"The Operator," says the soft voice, "will be offered a seat."

* * *

They vote.

It takes three hours. The Court's clerks go down the line with their rolls, and the Halls and clans answer one by one, and the count is called aloud in the cold. The Pill Hall: no. The Sutra Hall: no. The Law Hall: no. The Treasury, with its seat vacant, abstains. The Hall of Weights, in a whisper, abstains. The Cloud Peak Hall says no. The Tan say no. The Zhao say no. The Garden Hall says no, and Wenyuan's voice, deep and clear, rings off the Gate wall like a bell.

It is going well.

He has counted. By his own tally the noes are two hundred ahead, with the lower town still to come. He lets himself, for the first time in three days, breathe.

And then the clerk of the Council reads out the proxy.

He reads it from a slip of plum-bark, in a flat voice, in the snow. It is cast in the name of the Head of the Azure Cloud Sect, sealed with the Head's seal, witnessed by the Keeper of the Roll. It says Yes. It says Yes three times: for the Gate, for the Offering, and for the removal of the Elder of the Stair from his office, for cause, effective at the moment of the reading.

There is a short, dreadful pause.

Then the mask says gently: "The Head has spoken. The vote is carried. Elder Qin Hao, you are relieved of your post. The stair is the House's."

Qin Hao does not move from his stool. He is thinking, absurdly, of a young man of twenty-one carried up the Forty Steps on his brother's back, and of the way the stone had rung under the child's hand, and of the question he had not asked that day because he had been afraid of the answer. What are you? And the answer, he knows now, was not a name. It was a door.

* * *

It begins with a sound like a sheet tearing.

It comes from the snow. All round the Gate Court, between the ranks, in the gaps between the lamps, the drifts are splitting, and out of them, one after another, like blades drawn from a scabbard, rise the shadows. Tall. Thin. Black as ink. Each with a white tag on its breast. Dozens. A hundred. They come up out of the ground in silence and stand in a ring around the Court with their faceless heads bowed, and the crowd, which had been so quiet, makes a single low sound, like surf.

"Hold!" It is Mu. He has drawn the reforged blade, and its song is a thin high note in the dark. "Hold the line! Law Hall, to me!"

Then the Numbers move.

They are everywhere. They come out of the Halls' ranks with plain, quiet blades in their hands, wardens, clerks, tradesmen, a gatekeeper he once drank with, and they do not shout. They simply turn, and begin to cut. For a heartbeat the Court is a stunned and silent thing. Then the screaming begins.

"The wall!" Qin Hao is on his feet. He does not remember rising. His stool is somewhere behind him, and his knees are burning. "Bring them to the wall! Garden Hall, fall back! Back to the stair!"

He does not know whether they hear him. But he sees Wenyuan turn, tall and gray, and throw up an arm, and the three hundred and four close round the stair like a hand. He sees Feng at their head, with the quiet blade in his fist, and the circle of dullness spreading round him; a shadow reaches the edge of it and falters, and the Garden guards cut it down. He sees Bei, immense, with the iron bar of Kuang's last pupil, standing alone in the gap between two files and holding it with his bare back. He sees Yao and the Zhao, fifty-one, in a wedge. He sees Hu, roaring.

And he sees the Keeper, standing alone at the foot of the stair, not moving, not drawing, with its gloved hand still raised in the snow, as though the whole carnage were happening somewhere else.

Mu. He is on his knees. Where is Mu?

* * *

On the right of the stair, the Pill Hall holds.

Bai stands in the middle of his apprentices with a long iron spoon in one hand and a smoking clay jar in the other, and he is shouting. Qin Hao cannot hear the words. He sees the old man's round face red as a beet, his belly shaking, his plum-stained lips drawn back in what is certainly a curse, and then the jar leaves his hand in a long smoking arc and bursts among the nearest cluster of shadows. A cloud of sour yellow vapor rolls out. The shadows slow, and shiver, and come apart like wet paper. The apprentices cheer. Bai wipes his hands on his apron and reaches for another jar.

"Forty years of brewing!" he roars. "I've been saving it for a better occasion!"

Beside him, small and dreadful in her stiff white cloak, Ye has planted her stick in the snow. She is not fighting. She is reading. Her lips move, and from the frozen ground at her feet a ring of pale characters rises, glowing, line upon line, the old script of the Sutra Hall's oldest wards. They spread outward in a circle thirty paces wide. Where they touch a shadow, the shadow stops. Where they touch a Number, the Number's blade goes dull.

It is the last great ward of the Sutra Hall, and she has taken three years to prepare it. Qin Hao knows because he lent her the stone.

He thinks, with an odd clearness: We are not as few as I feared.

* * *

The Law Elder is at the center of the Court, in a ring of dead.

Qin Hao sees it as he is carried backward, pressed against the Gate wall by the crowd. There are nine bodies round Mu. Six are shadows, reduced to gray smoke; three are Numbers in the gray of the Treasury. The old man stands in their midst on legs that are failing, with his blade held low and blood running down his jaw from a gash across the temple. A tall figure in black is walking slowly toward him across the trampled snow: not a shadow, not a Number, but a woman in the dark cloak of an Enforcement Inspector, with a thin sword in her hand and a face of absolute calm.

"Mu Daoren," says Inspector Dai. "Number Forty-One. You are called to the House."

"I am not called."

"You are on the Roll."

"I have been struck from the Roll." Mu lifts his head. His iron eyes are bright. "By my own hand. At the Court's table, in the autumn. I put my name on a page, and drew a line through it, and gave it to the Arbiter. I did not belong to you, Dai. I was only counted."

"It is the same thing."

"No." The old man smiles. It is terrible. "It is not."

He moves.

It is the last thing Qin Hao sees of him that is whole: a short, hard, perfect lunge, the kind that a man makes once in forty years, with every ounce of what he has left. The reforged blade crosses the space in a line of silver. It takes the Inspector under the arm. She cries out, once, in what might be surprise. Her sword goes in at the same moment, and comes out through his back, and for a long heartbeat they stand together, their foreheads almost touching, like two old friends sharing a secret.

Then Mu sits down in the snow.

"I chose," he says, quite clearly. "The Rule."

His head falls.

* * *

"Elder!" It is Feng, at his shoulder. His face is black with smoke and his sleeve is red. "Elder Qin! The wall! The Gate Bearer is on the stair, and the House is coming down the steps behind us. We have perhaps a hundred breaths!"

Qin Hao turns.

At the head of the stair, in the open mouth of the Gate, a figure in gray stands on the topmost step with a pale blue bowl against his chest. His hair is tied back. His face is white. He is thirty-five, thin and straight, with a gray scarred arm and eyes like the winter sky, and in the bowl in his arms a small flame is burning, steady and gold. He is not looking at the fighting. He is looking at the Keeper.

And the Keeper, across forty paces of trampled snow and a ring of dead, has lowered its hand and turned its veiled head.

They are going to speak, thinks Qin Hao. They are going to speak, and everything will end.

"Jian!" he shouts.

The young man's head comes round.

"Go down!" The old man's voice cracks. "Go down! Shut the door! Do not come out until you are ready!"

"The clan—"

"The clan is mine. The wall is mine. I am the Elder of the Stair." He is already moving, stumbling, with Feng's arm under his shoulder, toward the Gate. "Do not argue with me, boy. I have been waiting sixty years to be told no, and I will not be told it tonight."

For a moment he thinks Jian will refuse.

Then something in the pale face changes. The young man looks, once, at the roaring Court, at his father in his ring of lanterns, at Yue and Bei and the Zhao wedge, and the old man sees him understand. Not what he must do. What it will cost.

Jian bows. It is a deep bow, a disciple's bow, held for a long time.

Then he turns, and goes down into the dark.

* * *

The wall is cold under his hand, and it knows him.

He has swept it every morning for sixty-three years. He has laid his palm on the ninth course and felt the hairline crack, and told himself that stone does not listen. But it does. He understands that now, as the hum comes up through his fingers and the whole great mass of the Gate answers him, block by block, like a hound that has heard its master's step.

He is leaning against it with his forehead on the granite and Feng's arm round his waist. Behind him the Court is a roar of steel and screaming. In front of him the stair mouth is open, a black square at the foot of the wall, and the last step is just vanishing into it.

"Elder," says Feng. "You cannot do this alone."

"I do not do it alone. I do it with the Gate."

"The Rule says the wall will close for the Elder of the Stair. It does not say what it takes."

"No." Qin Hao smiles, for the first time in perhaps ten years. "It does not."

He does not tell the boy what he knows. That the Founders built the wall to close only once. That the hand which seals it is the hand which holds it, and that a hand cannot let go of a wall. That there is, in the Rule of the Gate, a sentence that no one has read in six hundred years because no one has needed to, and that it begins: And the Elder shall be as the stone.

He thinks of the others, too, in the last moments left to him, in no order, as they come. A girl of fifteen in a cold yard, whom the Rule had said to continue. A tall old man with a wand of plum, who had cried at a table. A woman with a stick. A stout old physician who would not say thank you. A mother in a brown shawl, with silver in her hair, who had once pressed a bowl of rice into his hands without a word because she had seen him standing in the rain.

It is enough, he thinks. It was always enough. I only had to be asked.

He pushes Feng away.

"Go to your father."

"Elder—"

"Go. Take the clan. Take as many as you can reach. And when the House asks where the Gate Bearer is, tell them nothing." He lays both palms flat against the granite and closes his eyes. "Tell them the Elder of the Stair was at his post."

He hears Feng's footsteps recede. He hears, behind him, a high clear voice cry out his name: Yue's voice, perhaps, or a trick of the wind. He hears the roar of the Court. He hears the soft dry crackle of the shadows. He hears, very close, the footfall of the Keeper, unhurried, on the snow.

Then he hears nothing at all but the stone.

Close, he thinks.

The wall moves.

It does not grind. It does not shake. It simply moves, as a great animal moves, with a slow deep sigh. The forty-foot blocks slide, and the black square of the stair mouth narrows, and narrows, and the pale light of the lamps falls across it in a thinning bar. Qin Hao feels the cold go up his arms. He feels it reach his shoulders. His hands, flat against the granite, are no longer cold. They are not anything.

A voice speaks behind him.

It is soft, even, genderless, and very near. It says one word, a name he does not recognize, in a tone of absolute weariness.

"Qin."

He does not turn.

"You have done a very foolish thing," says the Keeper.

"Yes."

"It will take forty-nine days, perhaps, to understand how foolish."

"Perhaps." His lips are moving of their own accord. "But he is inside, and you are out."

There is a silence. The wall closes. The last bar of light narrows to a thread, and goes out.

And on the other side of the granite, in the dark, he feels a hand, gloved and light, laid very gently against the stone, exactly where his own is.
